name: Lungs
func: Bring oxygen into the blood and remove carbon dioxide. Air reaches about 300–500 million tiny air sacs (alveoli), where gas crosses a wall thinner than a soap bubble into the capillaries.

levels.kid:
You have two **lungs** inside your chest, one on each side of your heart. They're soft and spongy, like a pink sponge full of tiny balloons.

When you breathe in, air goes down a tube into your lungs and fills millions of those tiny balloons, called **alveoli**. Each one is wrapped in super-thin blood tubes. The **oxygen** from the air jumps into your blood, and your blood carries it all over your body so every part can make energy.

At the same time, your body's used-up air, called **carbon dioxide**, jumps from the blood into the balloons. When you breathe out, you blow it away.

Your ribs act like a cage that protects your lungs, and a big muscle underneath, the diaphragm, pulls down to help you breathe in.
levels.hs:
The lungs fill most of the **thoracic cavity**, one on each side of the **mediastinum** (the central space holding the heart, great vessels, trachea and esophagus). Each lung has an **apex** that rises about 2–3 cm above the clavicle into the root of the neck, and a concave **base** that rests on the **diaphragm**.

The **right lung** has **three lobes** (upper, middle, lower), separated by the **oblique** and **horizontal fissures**. The **left lung** has only **two lobes** (upper and lower) because it shares space with the heart; it has a **cardiac notch** and a tongue-like **lingula**.

Each lung is wrapped in a double membrane, the **pleura**. The **visceral pleura** sticks to the lung; the **parietal pleura** lines the chest wall. Between them is a thin film of fluid that lets them slide and keeps the lung stuck to the chest wall by surface tension, so when the chest expands the lung expands too.

Air travels trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → **alveoli**. With an alveolar surface of around 70 m² (roughly half a tennis court), gas exchange happens by **diffusion**: oxygen moves from high to low concentration into the blood, and carbon dioxide moves out.
levels.college:
Each lung connects to the mediastinum at its **root (hilum)**, where the main bronchus, pulmonary artery, two pulmonary veins, bronchial vessels, lymph nodes and the **pulmonary plexus** enter or leave. On the left the pulmonary artery sits highest at the hilum; on the right the **eparterial (upper lobe) bronchus** sits above the artery.

Lobes are divided into **bronchopulmonary segments** (10 on the right; 8–10 on the left, depending on whether some are counted as fused). Each segment has its own segmental bronchus and segmental branch of the pulmonary artery, with veins running between segments. That makes each segment surgically removable on its own.

The lungs have **two blood supplies**. The **pulmonary circulation** brings deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle at low pressure for gas exchange. The **bronchial arteries** (from the aorta) feed the lung tissue itself.

The respiratory zone begins at the **respiratory bronchioles**, then alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs and alveoli. The **blood–air barrier** is only about 0.5 µm thick: type I alveolar cell, fused basement membranes, capillary endothelium.

Breathing in is active: the diaphragm and external intercostals enlarge the chest, intrapleural pressure becomes more negative and air flows in. Quiet breathing out is mostly **passive elastic recoil**. Lymph drains toward the hilar and tracheobronchial nodes.

Surface landmarks matter in exams: the oblique fissure roughly follows the medial border of the scapula when the arm is raised overhead, and the horizontal fissure follows the 4th rib on the right.
levels.phd:
Alveoli are lined by two epithelial cell types. **Type I pneumocytes** cover about 95% of the surface area and are extremely thin, built for diffusion. **Type II pneumocytes** are cuboidal, make **surfactant** (mainly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine plus surfactant proteins SP-A, B, C and D) and act as **progenitors** that regenerate type I cells after injury. **Alveolar macrophages** patrol the airspace.

Surfactant lowers surface tension, more so as alveoli shrink. By the **Law of Laplace** (P = 2T/r), small alveoli would otherwise collapse into large ones; surfactant keeps them stable and reduces the work of breathing. SP-A and SP-D are collectins that also help innate immunity.

Gas exchange obeys **Fick's law**: transfer is proportional to area and partial-pressure gradient and inversely to thickness. Oxygen uptake at rest is normally **perfusion-limited**: blood is fully loaded about a third of the way along the capillary, leaving a reserve that thickened membranes (fibrosis) erode during exercise.

**Ventilation–perfusion (V/Q) matching** is the core idea. In an upright person both ventilation and perfusion increase toward the base, but perfusion more steeply, so V/Q is high at the apex and low at the base. **Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction**, unique to the lung, diverts blood away from poorly ventilated regions; it is mediated by oxygen-sensing mitochondria and potassium channels in pulmonary artery smooth muscle.

The lung is also a metabolic organ: endothelial **ACE** converts angiotensin I to II, and the pulmonary capillaries filter small clots. Research areas include single-cell atlases of the airway (which discovered the **pulmonary ionocyte**, rich in CFTR), lung organoids and regeneration after injury.
levels.expert:
**Examination**: inspection (rate, pattern, accessory muscle use), palpation (chest expansion, tracheal position, tactile fremitus), percussion and auscultation. Classic patterns:
- **Consolidation (pneumonia)**: dull percussion, **bronchial breath sounds**, increased vocal resonance, crackles, sometimes **egophony** ("ee" sounds like "ay").
- **Pleural effusion**: **stony dull** percussion, reduced breath sounds and fremitus.
- **Pneumothorax**: **hyper-resonant** percussion, absent breath sounds; in **tension pneumothorax** the trachea deviates **away**, with low blood pressure, and it is an emergency treated by immediate decompression.
- **Collapse**: trachea pulled **toward** the affected side.
- **Fibrosis**: fine "velcro" crackles at the bases, often with **clubbing**.

**Imaging**: chest X-ray first (look for the **silhouette sign**: loss of the right heart border means right middle lobe disease, loss of a hemidiaphragm means lower lobe disease), then **CT** (high-resolution CT for interstitial disease, CT pulmonary angiography for **pulmonary embolism**). **Spirometry** separates obstructive (FEV1/FVC reduced, as in asthma and COPD) from restrictive patterns.

An **apical (Pancoast) tumour** can invade the lower brachial plexus and the sympathetic chain, causing arm pain, hand weakness and **Horner syndrome**. Lung cancer is also the commonest source of **brain metastases**, so neurosurgeons see a lot of it, and small cell carcinoma causes paraneoplastic syndromes such as **Lambert–Eaton** and SIADH.

**Surgery** removes a wedge, segment (**segmentectomy**), lobe (**lobectomy**) or whole lung (**pneumonectomy**), often by video-assisted (VATS) or robotic thoracoscopy. Chest drains are placed in the "**safe triangle**" in the 4th–5th intercostal space at the mid-axillary line, just above a rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle running under the rib above.

keyPoints: Right lung has 3 lobes, left has 2 (with cardiac notch and lingula)
Pleura: visceral on lung, parietal on chest wall
Bronchopulmonary segments are independent surgical units
Type I cells for diffusion, type II make surfactant
Hypoxic vasoconstriction matches blood to ventilation
Tension pneumothorax pushes the trachea away

test.q: How many lobes does the left lung have?
test.explain: The left lung has upper and lower lobes; the heart takes up the space where a middle lobe would be.

test.q: Which alveolar cells make surfactant? Type ___ pneumocytes.
test.explain: Type II pneumocytes make surfactant and can regenerate type I cells.

test.q: Which finding fits a large pleural effusion?
test.explain: Fluid in the pleural space makes percussion stony dull and muffles breath sounds.

test.q: In the lung, low oxygen in an alveolus makes its blood vessels:
test.explain: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts blood to well-ventilated alveoli. Elsewhere in the body, hypoxia dilates vessels.

test.q: An apical lung tumour that invades the brachial plexus and sympathetic chain is called a ______ tumour.
test.explain: Pancoast tumours sit at the apex and can cause Horner syndrome plus arm pain and weakness.
